### Problem: Three Parts of the Array {#sec-pref-p6-b}

::: {.p-statement}
An array $d$ of $n$ **positive** integers ($1 \le n \le 2\cdot10^5$, $1 \le d_i \le 10^9$). Split it into three contiguous parts — first $a$ elements, next $b$, last $c$, any of them possibly empty, every element in exactly one part — maximising $\text{sum}_1$ subject to $\text{sum}_1 = \text{sum}_3$. Print that maximum sum.

Source: [CF 1006C · Three Parts of the Array](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1006/C){.solved rating="1200"}
:::

::: {.p-intuition}
Two cuts, three sums. Because every value is positive, the left sum only grows as its cut moves right, and the right sum only grows as its cut moves *left* — so the two cuts travel in one direction each and never need to be revisited. That monotonicity is what turns an $O(n^2)$ pair scan into $O(n)$, and it is exactly the property that LC 2270 above did not have.
:::

::: {.p-approach}
1. **Brute force.** Try all $(i, j)$ with $0 \le i \le j \le n$: $O(n^2)$ cuts, each tested in $O(1)$ with the prefix table — still about $\frac{n^2}{2} = 2\cdot10^{10}$ tests.
2. **Prefix table + two pointers.** Fix the left cut at $i$; the right cut $j$ must satisfy $P[n]-P[j] = P[i]$. As $i$ increases the target right sum increases, so $j$ only ever decreases. Grow the right part (`while` its sum is still below the left sum) and record a match: $O(n)$.
3. Equivalent: for each $i$ binary search $P$ for the value $P[n]-P[i]$ in the window $[i, n]$, $O(n\log n)$ and slightly easier to get right. The two-pointer version is what the monotonicity buys you.

**Invariant.** After the `while` loop for left cut $i$, $j$ is the largest cut with $j \ge i$ whose right part $P[n]-P[j]$ is at least $P[i]$ (or $j = i$ if there is none). Because $P[i]$ only grows with $i$ and the right part only grows as $j$ falls, that $j$ can only move left, so no candidate is ever skipped. `best` is the largest $\text{sum}_1$ of a *verified* pair $(i,j)$ with $i\le j$, so the middle part $a[i{:}j]$ never has negative length.
:::

The buttons are in order. Each one keeps the previous solution and changes only what that form changes.

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Try every pair of cuts

::: {.form-next}
Two cuts $i \le j$ give three parts; test $P[i] = P[n]-P[j]$ for all $\binom{n+1}{2}$ pairs, each read in $O(1)$ from the table. Honest and $O(n^2)$ — about $2\cdot10^{10}$ pairs at the limits, because moving $i$ one step re-scans every possible $j$.
:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
def three_parts_brute(a):
    n = len(a)
    p = build_prefix(a)
    best = 0
    for i in range(n + 1):
        for j in range(i, n + 1):
            if p[i] == p[n] - p[j]:
                best = max(best, p[i])
    return best
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <vector>
#include <algorithm>
using namespace std;

long long threePartsBrute(const vector<long long>& a) {
    int n = (int)a.size();
    vector<long long> p(n + 1, 0);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) p[i + 1] = p[i] + a[i];
    long long best = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i <= n; ++i)
        for (int j = i; j <= n; ++j)
            if (p[i] == p[n] - p[j]) best = max(best, p[i]);
    return best;
}
```
:::

#### Two pointers, one shared table

::: {.form-next}
Every value is **positive**, so `left` $=P[i]$ grows with $i$ while the right part $P[n]-P[j]$ grows as $j$ moves left. Fix $i$ and walk a single $j$ backwards until the right part reaches `left` — $j$ never moves forward, so the pair scan collapses to $O(n)$. This is exactly the monotonicity LC 2270 above could not assume.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("split3", "pointers")
    assert str(final) == "5"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}
##### Python

```{python}
#| label: arr-three-parts
def three_parts(a: list[int]) -> int:
    n = len(a)
    p = build_prefix(a)
    total = p[n]
    best, j = 0, n                          # right part is a[j:n]
    for i in range(n + 1):
        left = p[i]
        while j > i and total - p[j] < left:
            j -= 1                          # grow the right part
        if j >= i and total - p[j] == left:
            best = max(best, left)          # middle a[i:j] may be empty
    return best


for _ in range(400):
    a = [random.randint(1, 9) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 11))]
    assert three_parts(a) == three_parts_brute(a)

assert three_parts([1, 3, 1, 1, 4]) == 5      # the board sample: [1,3,1] | [] | [1,4]
assert three_parts([1, 3, 2, 1, 4]) == 4      # [1,3] | [2,1] | [4]
assert three_parts([4, 1, 2]) == 0            # only the empty-everything match
assert three_parts([2, 2]) == 2               # [2] | [] | [2]
assert three_parts([1]) == 0
print("three_parts OK")
```

##### C++

```cpp
#include <bits/stdc++.h>
using namespace std;

int main() {
    ios::sync_with_stdio(false); cin.tie(nullptr);
    int n; cin >> n;
    vector<long long> p(n + 1, 0);
    for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) { long long x; cin >> x; p[i + 1] = p[i] + x; }
    long long best = 0;
    int j = n;
    for (int i = 0; i <= n; ++i) {
        long long left = p[i];
        while (j > i && p[n] - p[j] < left) --j;         // grow the right part
        if (j >= i && p[n] - p[j] == left) best = max(best, left);
    }
    cout << best << '\n';
}
```
:::
:::

::: {.p-complexity}
**Try every pair of cuts** is $O(n^2)$ — about $2\cdot10^{10}$ pairs at the limits — with $O(n)$ for the table. **Two pointers, one shared table** is $O(n)$: $i$ moves forward $n+1$ times and $j$ moves backward at most $n+1$ times in total, the two-pointer amortisation of @sec-arr-scan applied to cut positions instead of window edges (the binary-search variant is $O(n\log n)$). **Space** $O(n)$ for the table, or $O(1)$ if you keep both running sums as variables. Sums reach $2\cdot10^{14}$: 64-bit throughout (@sec-arr-cost).
:::

::: {.p-edge}
- Empty parts are legal: $i = 0$ and $j = n$ give $\text{sum}_1=\text{sum}_3=0$, which is why `best` starts at $0$ and why a "no answer" case is never a $-1$.
- $n = 1$: the only equal split is the empty one, answer $0$. $n = 2$ with equal values gives $[x] \mid [\,] \mid [x]$, answer $x$.
- Positivity is load-bearing: with negatives, `left` is not monotone in $i$, `j` would have to move back and forth, and the $O(n)$ argument collapses to the $O(n^2)$ pair scan — the same audit as in @sec-pref-p6-a.
- `total` odd makes equality impossible for a middle-empty split, but not for others; never shortcut with `total / 2` integer division.
:::
